prompt: The display name says 'Examplebank Support'. What should you check to learn who really sent the email?
options: The actual sender address
The font
The time it was sent
The size of the email
explanation: Anyone can type any display name. The address inside the angle brackets shows who really sent it.

prompt: An email comes from support@examplebank-secure.co. What does that tell you?
options: It is from Examplebank, because it contains the name
The domain is different from the bank's own, so it is suspicious
Domains ending in .co are always safe
The word secure means it is safe
explanation: The name is inside a different domain. Attackers add words like secure to look official.

prompt: The link text reads www.examplebank.com, but hovering over it shows a completely different address. What should you do?
options: Trust the text, because it shows the bank
Trust the hover address, so do not click
Click, because it is probably a browser bug
Click, because it is just a tracking link
explanation: Link text can say anything. The real destination is what matters, and a mismatch is a strong warning sign.

prompt: Which attachment deserves the most suspicion?
options: An unexpected .zip archive claiming to be an invoice
A meeting invitation from a colleague you spoke with this morning
A PDF a colleague sends right after discussing it on a call
A photo from a family member's usual address after you asked for it
explanation: Unexpected archives are a common way to deliver malware. The others were expected, which makes them much less suspicious.

prompt: An email from 'IT Helpdesk' shows an internal From address, but its Reply-To is it.helpdesk.team@outlook-mail.co. What does this mean?
options: Replies would go to an outside address, which is a warning sign
Reply-To is only decoration
IT uses it to protect privacy
Nothing, because the From address looks internal
explanation: The From line can be made to look internal. A different Reply-To sends your answer, possibly a password, to an outsider.

prompt: You ordered nothing. An email says: 'Dear customer, your parcel could not be delivered. Pay $1.99 within 12 hours.' Which red flags are present?
options: Generic greeting, an unexpected delivery, and a deadline
Only a spelling mistake
None, because small fees are always genuine
Only that it is in your inbox
explanation: A vague greeting, a delivery you did not expect, and a deadline for a tiny fee are classic signs. The real goal is your card details.

prompt: An email has perfect spelling and a professional design. What does that tell you?
options: That it is safe
Nothing, so you should still check the sender, links and request
That it was written by a native speaker, so it is real
That it came from a large company
explanation: Polish proves nothing. Modern tools can produce flawless text, so judge the request, the sender and the link.

prompt: A colleague's real address emails you: 'Please review the attached invoice, urgent.' It is out of character and you were not expecting it. What is the best action?
options: Open it, because it is from a colleague
Message or call the colleague on a channel you know to confirm
Forward it to the whole team to ask
Open it in a private browser window
explanation: A colleague's account may have been hacked. An out-of-character request deserves a quick check through another channel.
